title: Building our own physics
summary: A50–A51: from cylinder energy to pressure-driven gas transfer.

sections.title: A component before an engine
sections.text: After testing how a small model learned from commercial calculations, Wahoo turned to a different question: could it build an original physical component whose equations and numerical behaviour could be checked directly? A50 began with a single gas-filled cylinder. A51 added one pressure-driven restriction. Both were deliberately smaller than a complete engine model. Their accepted results concern synthetic ideal-gas experiments, not measured Wahoo performance. This narrow starting point made it possible to compare calculations with analytical references, expose numerical weaknesses and define what the next component would need to solve. The milestone was ownership of inspectable, tested physics software, with its limits recorded alongside its capabilities.

sections.title: Accounting for what enters and leaves
sections.text: The A50 kernel tracks gas mass and internal energy as a cylinder changes volume. Heat can enter; expanding gas can do work; prescribed inflow and outflow can carry mass and energy. Pressure and temperature follow the declared ideal-gas relationships. These terms must remain consistent: an apparently plausible pressure curve is insufficient if the underlying energy balance is wrong. The implementation used original Python code and adaptive fourth-order integration. It reused accepted nominal slider-crank geometry: a 54 mm bore, 54.5 mm stroke and 102 mm connecting rod. The analytical fixtures supplied their own synthetic clearance and operating conditions. In particular, an 8 cc test clearance was not an accepted physical Wahoo chamber specification.

sections.title: Testing against something independent
sections.text: A50 was checked on twelve analytical fixture instances covering closed gas, moving volume, prescribed heat and transport, with ten kernel unit tests and explicit expected-failure outputs. Independent references compared the saved states and accumulated work, heat and enthalpy. The largest scaled state error in the checked fixtures was approximately 2.37 billionths, below the frozen target. A smooth-forcing refinement test showed the expected fourth-order pattern as resolution increased. Those are results for the stated tests, not a universal accuracy guarantee. A separate coarse plotting-grid energy calculation failed its accuracy target and remained recorded. The accepted conservation evidence came from analytical comparisons, rather than treating agreement between bookkeeping counters as proof that the physics was correct.

sections.title: Letting pressure drive the flow
sections.text: A51 replaced a prescribed transfer rate with a calculated one through a fixed restriction. Higher pressure determines the donor side, including which temperature supplies the transported enthalpy. Flow can reverse. At equal pressures, pressure-driven transfer is exactly zero even if temperatures differ. A geometric area and an explicit discharge coefficient remain separate inputs. The formulation covers subcritical flow and the sonic plateau reached when lower downstream pressure can no longer increase the idealized flow rate. This choking condition is not a resolved jet or a complete Mach-number field. The reservoirs approximate stagnation conditions because bulk velocity is neglected. Coupled tests then connected that restriction to A50 storage, so mass and energy changed together rather than through an externally imposed schedule.

sections.title: The failures made the boundary clearer
sections.text: Independent review found an extreme-input overflow defect after the initial standalone tests had passed. Its wrong finite result and source were preserved; corrected arithmetic then passed the retained robustness checks. A reversal test exposed a separate weakness in the independent quadrature diagnostic, repaired through event-aware integration without changing the production physics or acceptance threshold. Near pressure equalization, three tested tolerance settings failed strict wrong-way transport limits despite calm saved pressure curves. Exactly one prospectively frozen tighter setting passed. It required 70,384 accepted steps and 17 rejected attempts for only 0.02 seconds of synthetic evolution, taking about 28.47 seconds of wall time. The passing reverse-enthalpy result had an 8.86 percent margin. Acceptance therefore demonstrated a bounded, tolerance-specific result while revealing a serious efficiency problem.

sections.title: What the accepted gates actually mean
sections.text: Independent review accepted all four A50 gates and all four A51 gates within their declared synthetic scopes. A51 demonstrated standalone restriction behaviour and coupling cases including discharge, filling, continuous reversal, a finite pair and moving slider volume. It did not qualify efficient general equalization or a complete engine cycle. Actual piston-controlled ports, real reed dynamics, calibrated discharge coefficients, scavenging, combustion, thermal behaviour, exhaust waves and shaft power still required further work. No horsepower ranking or manufacturing release followed. The next recommendation was to handle equalization and donor switching efficiently before adding changing port areas. That sequence matters: expanding a model is useful only when each new layer inherits a foundation whose mathematical checks, retained failures and physical assumptions can still be understood. The work establishes a starting point for that development, with physical engine validity explicitly still on hold.
